deposits.genre_observed: effective act / diagnostic working draft on the aorist and English aspect

finds.quote: English has operated for centuries without a true non-indexed perfective. This absence is not accidental. It was produced by the material conditions of legal administration, labor discipline, colonial record-keeping, and capital accumulation—all of which required temporally indexed action.
finds.note: Argued historical-material thesis: the absence of a non-indexed perfective in English was produced by legal administration, labor discipline, colonial record-keeping and capital accumulation; developed through Part II (PIE > Latin > Germanic > ME > EModE) and Part III; the deposit proposes no direct test of the historical causation (Part IV tests the synchronic gap).

finds.quote:
Why did Latin do this? Several hypotheses:

**Administrative efficiency:** Roman legal and bureaucratic language needed clear temporal indexing. When did the contract form? When did the crime occur? The aorist's temporal vagueness was a liability in legal contexts.

**Contact influence:** Latin's contact with Italic and Etruscan languages may have favored the merger.

**The rise of written record-keeping:** Oral cultures can tolerate aspectual nuance because context disambiguates. Written administrative cultures need explicit temporal markers.
finds.note: Causal thesis on why Latin merged aorist and perfect (administrative/legal need for temporal indexing; written record-keeping), offered as hypotheses and taken up by the deposit's argument in Part III.
